item.title: Two ends of a folktale archive: Sagenland and Nachtdienst
item.description: During my PhD, I got to work with the Dutch Folktale Database, the Nederlandse Volksverhalenbank at the Meertens Institute. At the time it contained around 45,000 stories in various genres collected in the Netherlands. A few years back the database, manintained and developed by Theo Meder, was merged with the Flemish Folktale Database, enlarging it to over 100k stories. With over 40,000 different attestations, the most prominent genre in this renewed database – the Folktale Database of the Low Countries – is the legend: devils at crossroads, white women on the heath, will-o’-the-wisps over the bog, the neighbour who could bewitch your cows. In recent work I have been exploring the effect of collection and collector bias on the representation of cultural diversity. Here too, it is tempting to read that collection as a picture of what people in the Low Countries told each other. But every record in it went through a chain of hands. Someone told the story. A collector cycled to a farm, sat down at a kitchen table, asked the right question and wrote down the answer. Back at the archive, someone typed the record, decided what kind of story it was, gave it a number and filed it in a (digital) drawer.

item.title: Estimating Unseen Shared Cultural Diversity
item.description:
Shared Species Estimation

In Demystifying Chao1 with Good-Turing, I tried to explain the intuition behind the Chao1 estimator (Chao 1984) for unseen species using the Good-Turing estimator as described in Chao et al. (2017). The latter article discusses another set of diversity measures within that same framework of Turing. The number of unique species or the number of unique cultural artifacts in a given environment is only one diversity measure, but we can also study the shared diversity between two cultural collections, for example. In addition to the number of unique species, this definition of diversity thus also involves the specific composition of an assemblage or collection. As with estimating the number of unique species, it is quite conceivable that our samples do not give a complete picture of which species or cultural artifacts are shared between two assemblages or collections. Fortunately, with only a few small adjustments, we can modify the Good-Turing framework to compute a lower-bound on the number of unseen items shared between two collections.
